## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

## What the current top five says about changing American dog ownership
Credit: Andres Ayrton / Pexels
Five breeds make up the current top five: the French Bulldog, the Labrador Retriever, the Golden Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog, and the Dachshund. Looked at together, they split into two different kinds of dog — small companions suited to close quarters, and medium-to-large breeds developed for work in open country. That split is the clearest pattern in the AKC's annual count of America's most popular dog breeds.
The small end of the list has gained the most ground. The French Bulldog and the Dachshund both fit in a one-bedroom apartment, cost less to feed than a 70-pound retriever, and do not need a yard to stay settled. Neither reached the top five by replacing a breed already sliding out of it; each got there by passing dogs that had held those positions for years.
The larger breeds have not collapsed in response. A Labrador, a Golden Retriever, or a German Shepherd still does things a small companion cannot: retrieving birds from cold water, detection work, guide work, or covering miles of trail beside a runner. Households that hunt, run, farm, or want a dog built for formal training keep registering them in volume, which is why three of the five slots belong to breeds that need real daily exercise.
The German Shepherd sits in its own category here. Its draw is guarding instinct and aptitude for structured work rather than an easygoing family temperament, and it remains the breed most associated with police, military, and search-and-rescue handling in the U.S.
Taken together, the five describe a country sorting dogs by the space and time it has for them. Size, grooming load, exercise needs, trainability, and tolerance for small living quarters pull in different directions, and no single factor explains the full ranking. The registration data shows steady movement toward compact breeds at the edges of the top five, alongside decades of continuous demand for the versatile sporting and working dogs that dominated the list for most of the modern era.

Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

Credit: Andres Ayrton / Pexels
Five breeds make up the current top five: the French Bulldog, the Labrador Retriever, the Golden Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog, and the Dachshund. That split is the clearest pattern in the AKC's annual count of America's most popular dog breeds.
The small end of the list has gained the most ground. The French Bulldog and the Dachshund both fit in a one-bedroom apartment, cost less to feed than a 70-pound retriever, and do not need a yard to stay settled. Neither reached the top five by replacing a breed already sliding out of it; each got there by passing dogs that had held those positions for years.
The larger breeds have not collapsed in response. A Labrador, a Golden Retriever, or a German Shepherd still does things a small companion cannot: retrieving birds from cold water, detection work, guide work, or covering miles of trail beside a runner. Households that hunt, run, farm, or want a dog built for formal training keep registering them in volume, which is why three of the five slots belong to breeds that need real daily exercise.
The German Shepherd sits in its own category here. Its draw is guarding instinct and aptitude for structured work rather than an easygoing family temperament, and it remains the breed most associated with police, military, and search-and-rescue handling in the U.S.
Taken together, the five describe a country sorting dogs by the space and time it has for them. Size, grooming load, exercise needs, trainability, and tolerance for small living quarters pull in different directions, and no single factor explains the full ranking. By ABC News
March 28, 2018, 9:01 AM
Labrador retrievers are the most popular dog breed in the United States, but perhaps not for long.
The French bulldog could soon take their place on the American Kennel Club (AKC)’s annual list of most popular dog breeds.
Bulldogs William Wonka, 14-weeks, left, and Dailey, 2, pose for photographers during a news conference at the American Kennel Club headquarters, March 28, 2018, in New York. American Kennel Club rankings released in 2018 show bulldogs are the fifth most popular purebred dog.
Mary Altaffer/AP
The French bulldog climbed into the top four last year, knocking the Beagle out of the top five for the first time in nearly 20 years.
The 2017 list was released today by the AKC.
“The French bulldog is poised for a takeover,” AKC Executive Secretary Gina DiNardo said in a statement, noting the breed’s “adaptability” and “loveable temperament.”
The Labrador retriever though has held the top ranking in AKC’s list for 27 years, a feat DiNardo attributed to the breed’s versatility and family-friendly nature.

Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2014
By AKC Staff
Updated: Jan 22, 2018 | 2 Minutes
Updated: Jan 22, 2018 | 2 Minutes
The Labrador Retriever has done it again.
The intelligent, family friendly breed held onto the number one spot on the most popular list for the 24th consecutive year, continuing the longest reign as the nation’s top dog in American Kennel Club history.
For the full list of breed rankings, clickhere.
While the Lab holds strong, the Bulldog has quietly crept up the list, landing this year at number four for the first time. This is the highest ranking in the breed's history. Bulldogs make excellent family companions with a natural tendency to form strong bonds with children, an easy-to-care-for coat, and minimal exercise requirements.
Meanwhile, the popular French Bulldog continues its quest for the number one spot, breaking into the top 10 for the first time in nearly 100 years. This year the Frenche finds himself at number nine, knocking the Dachshund out of the top 10 for the first time since 1985.
“The Lab truly is America’s dog,” said AKC Vice President Gina DiNardo, “but the lovable Bulldog breeds are clamoring to dominate. Watch out for an upset next year.”
America’s most popular breeds aren’t the only movers and shakers this year. The Wirehaired Pointing Griffon made huge strides over the past decade, jumping 38 spots from 112th in 2004 to 74th in 2014.
Other breeds making double-digit gains over the past decade include the Havanese (from 52nd in 2004 to 25th in 2014), the Border Collie (from 60th in 2004 to 39th in 2014), the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever (from 118th in 2004 to 96th in 2014), and the Black and Tan Coonhound (from 140th in 2004 to 120th in 2014).

2. German Shepherd Dog

4. Bulldog

5. Beagle

6. Yorkshire Terrier

7. Poodle

8. Boxer

By Radhika Chalasani
February 26, 2015 / 11:07 PM EST / CBS News
Add CBS News on Google
Getty Images/iStockphoto
America's reigning most popular dog breed is still the labrador retriever for the 24th year in 2014, but bulldogs are making a race for the top.
Check outthe American Kennel Club's (AKC) 10 most popular breeds. One of them may be your next or current best friend.
Labrador retrievers hit the top 10 list in the 1970s and haven't left since. They broke the poodles' decade-old record in 2013.

## No. 1: Labrador retriever
iStock
Gina DiNardo, the American Kennel Club's vice president, said, "the lab truly is America's dog."
You can take your pick of black lab, yellow lab or chocolate lab.

## No. 2: German shepherd
iStock
The German shepherd is hanging tough, retaining its number two spot on the American Kennel Club's list of of 10 most popular dog breeds for 2014.
American Kennel Club
The first impression of a German shepherd is that of a strong, agile, well muscled animal.
It was first officially recognized by the AKC in 1908.

## No. 3: Golden retriever
American Kennel Club
The golden retriever has always been a popular breed and is ranked number 3 by the American Kennel Club for 2014.
iStock
Overall, AKC has leaned toward larger dogs in the past decade and the golden retriever is no exception.

## No. 4: Bulldog
iStock
The bulldog quietly crept up the list to number 4 -- the highest ranking in the breed's history.
American Kennel Club
The bulldog's rise in the top 10 hasn't been a surprise to their fans who extol their unmistakable, push-faced expressions and generally calm manner.

## No. 5: Beagle
iStock
The beagle, a happy, inquisitive short-haired hound, ranked number 5 on the list of most popular dog breeds for 2014 by the AKC.
American Kennel Club
Beagles are small, compact, and hardy dogs.They're scent hounds used primarily for hunting rabbits to larger hares.
The breed was officially recognized in 1885 by the AKC.

## No. 6: Yorkshire terrier
iStock
The Yorkshire terrier didn't quite make it into the top 5, retaining its number 6 spot on the list from 2013.
American Kennel Club
Although the AKC has leaned towards larger dogs in the past decade, small breed Yorkies still held on to number 6 on the top 10 list.

## No. 7: Poodle
iStock
The poodle once reigned supreme, but is now ranked number 7 by the AKC for 2014.
The poodle's decades-old record as the most popular breed ended in 2013 when it was surpassed by the labrador retriever.
American Kennel Club
The poodle ranked number 7 for 2014 by the AKC, moving up a spot from 8th place.
The denominations standard, miniature, and toy are used to describe size only. All poodles are one breed.

## No. 8: Boxer
iStock
Coming in at number 8 on the list is the boxer.
The high energy, medium-sized dog was developed to serve as a guard, working, and companion dog.
American Kennel Club
The boxer has been described as the "George Clooney" of the dog world, a hunk with a sense of humor and an underlying sweetness.

## No. 9: French bulldog
American Kennel Club
The French bulldog's continued quest for the number one spot gained traction as it broke into the top 10 list for the first time in nearly 100 years.
iStock
The comical, playful French bulldog entered the top ten list in 2014 after a decade-long popularity spurt and now ranks 9th.
Frenchies, recognized by the AKC in 1898, are indoor dogs and require air conditioning in warm weather.

# The Most Popular Dog Breeds of 2014
By AKC Staff
Updated: Jan 22, 2018 | 2 Minutes
Updated: Jan 22, 2018 | 2 Minutes
The Labrador Retriever has done it again.
The intelligent, family friendly breed held onto the number one spot on the most popular list for the 24th consecutive year, continuing the longest reign as the nation’s top dog in American Kennel Club history.
For the full list of breed rankings, clickhere.
While the Lab holds strong, the Bulldog has quietly crept up the list, landing this year at number four for the first time. This is the highest ranking in the breed's history. Bulldogs make excellent family companions with a natural tendency to form strong bonds with children, an easy-to-care-for coat, and minimal exercise requirements.
Meanwhile, the popular French Bulldog continues its quest for the number one spot, breaking into the top 10 for the first time in nearly 100 years. This year the Frenche finds himself at number nine, knocking the Dachshund out of the top 10 for the first time since 1985.
“The Lab truly is America’s dog,” said AKC Vice President Gina DiNardo, “but the lovable Bulldog breeds are clamoring to dominate. Watch out for an upset next year.”
America’s most popular breeds aren’t the only movers and shakers this year. The Wirehaired Pointing Griffon made huge strides over the past decade, jumping 38 spots from 112th in 2004 to 74th in 2014.
Other breeds making double-digit gains over the past decade include the Havanese (from 52nd in 2004 to 25th in 2014), the Border Collie (from 60th in 2004 to 39th in 2014), the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever (from 118th in 2004 to 96th in 2014), and the Black and Tan Coonhound (from 140th in 2004 to 120th in 2014).
